name: Amoxicillin
dosage: 500mg every 8 hours or 875mg every 12 hours for adults.
defenseContext: Standard issue in field medical kits for broad-spectrum bacterial infections. Ensure patient has no penicillin allergy before administration.

name: Ibuprofen
defenseContext: Primary non-opioid analgesic for combat-related minor injuries and sprains. Take with food if possible.

name: Epinephrine (Adrenalin)
defenseContext: Critical lifesaving medication. All personnel should carry auto-injectors in high-risk environments. Administer immediately upon signs of severe allergic reaction.

name: Morphine Sulfate
defenseContext: Used for severe trauma pain. Monitor respiratory rate closely. Naloxone must be available.

name: Naloxone (Narcan)
dosage: 0.4-2mg IV/IM/SC/IN, repeat every 2-3 minutes if necessary.
defenseContext: Essential for counteracting opioid-induced respiratory depression. Carried by medics for immediate deployment.

name: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
dosage: 1g over 10 minutes IV, followed by 1g over 8 hours.
defenseContext: Critical for treating combat casualties with severe bleeding. Administer within 3 hours of injury for maximum effectiveness.

name: Atropine
dosage: 2mg IM every 5-15 minutes until secretions dry (for nerve agents).
defenseContext: Component of nerve agent antidote kits (e.g., ATNAA). Administer immediately upon exposure to chemical nerve agents.

name: Ciprofloxacin
dosage: 500mg every 12 hours for 60 days for anthrax.
defenseContext: Stockpiled for biological warfare defense, particularly against inhaled anthrax. Use with caution during intense physical activity due to tendon rupture risk.

name: Ketamine
dosage: 0.5 to 1 mg/kg IV or 2 to 4 mg/kg IM.
defenseContext: Preferred analgesic and anesthetic in combat environments where airway management is difficult, as it preserves respiratory drive.

name: Moxifloxacin
defenseContext: Part of the Combat Wound Pill Pack (CWPP). Taken orally by conscious casualties with penetrating injuries to prevent infection.

name: Meloxicam
defenseContext: Part of the Combat Wound Pill Pack (CWPP) for pain control in conscious casualties who can swallow. Does not alter platelet function as significantly as aspirin.

name: Ceftriaxone
defenseContext: Used at forward surgical teams for severe trauma and open wounds. Broad spectrum coverage.

name: Fentanyl Citrate (Actiq)
defenseContext: Administered via transmucosal lozenge (lollipop) for rapid pain relief on the battlefield. Easy to remove from patient's mouth if respiratory depression occurs.

name: Diazepam (Valium)
dosage: 5-10mg IV/IM for seizures or nerve agent exposure.
defenseContext: Included in the CANA (Convulsant Antidote for Nerve Agent) auto-injector. Administered after Atropine to prevent or stop seizures from nerve agents.

name: Doxycycline
defenseContext: Standard issue for malaria prophylaxis in deployed troops. Also stockpiled as an alternative treatment for anthrax exposure. Troops must be warned about sun sensitivity.

name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
defenseContext: Used to treat nausea associated with trauma, transport (medevac), or administration of strong opioids like Morphine.

name: Lidocaine 1%
dosage: Infiltrate locally as needed. Max 4.5 mg/kg.
defenseContext: Essential for field suturing, chest tube placement, or other minor surgical interventions at aid stations.

name: Ertapenem
defenseContext: Often used in combat casualty care for patients with severe penetrating injuries who cannot take oral medications (alternative to Moxifloxacin).

name: Pralidoxime (2-PAM)
defenseContext: Included in the Mark I kit or ATNAA alongside Atropine. Essential for reactivating cholinesterase enzymes blocked by nerve agents.

name: Calcium Gluconate
dosage: Apply topically for HF burns or 1-2g IV for hyperkalemia.
defenseContext: Used for specific chemical burns (hydrofluoric acid) which can occur in maintenance or industrial military settings.
